topics: 🪵 Whole Vessels vs. Broken Ones — Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on kindling with date pits and nutshells
🧦 Small Cloths and Set-Aside — how discarding into the trash, hanging on a peg, or boxing a rag changes its status
🥚 New Mishna: The Pierced Eggshell — an indirect oil-drip banned by the Rabbis, permitted by Rabbi Yehuda
🏛️ The House of Nitza Story — Rabbi Yehuda's proof from Rabbi Tarfon's silence, and why it was rejected
🪑 Dragging Furniture on Shabbat — Rabbi Shimon's leniency and the dispute over large versus small pieces

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Broken Vessels, a Dripping Eggshell, and a New Mishna on Extinguishing
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 29a–29b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא יִקּוֹב אָדָם שְׁפוֹפֶרֶת שֶׁל בֵּיצָה וִימַלְּאֶנָּה שֶׁמֶן וְיִתְּנֶנָּה עַל פִּי הַנֵּר בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁתְּהֵא מְנַטֶּפֶת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues examining the folded-wick mishna's underlying dispute, testing why Rav Yosef's 'three by three exactly' matters and why Rabbi Yehuda restricts kindling to whole, not broken, vessels — extending this to date pits and nutshells, each teaching a case that could not be derived from the others. A second explanation, from Rav Hamnuna, roots Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Akiva's dispute in a Kelim mishna about small cloths used for menial tasks, and whether tossing, hanging, or boxing a rag negates its garment-status. A new mishna then forbids indirect methods of feeding a Shabbat lamp more oil — a pierced eggshell or an adjacent oil bowl — which Rabbi Yehuda permits; the Gemara illustrates with Rabbi Yehuda's own story from the house of Nitza in Lod, and a related discussion of dragging furniture on Shabbat. The daf ends with a fresh mishna on extinguishing a lamp: exempt when done from fear or for a sick person's sake, but liable when done to spare the lamp, oil, or wick.

slides.title: 🪵 Rabbi Yehuda's Three 'Nolad' Cases
slides.subtitle: Each teaches something the others could not
rows: Forbidden — became 'newly created' (nolad) when they broke
Forbidden — were hidden in the fruit, now exposed
Forbidden — even though shells were always exposed

callout.label: Why all three were needed:
callout.text: Vessels alone might suggest only 'transformed' items are forbidden; pits alone might suggest only 'newly exposed' items are forbidden; shells prove the prohibition is broader still, since they were exposed all along.

slides.title: 🧦 A Small Cloth: When Does It Stop Being a 'Garment'?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva's shifting position

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: A cloth under three-by-three handbreadths, used to plug a bath or wipe a millstone: R' Eliezer says it can become impure whether or not it was set aside for that use.

lines.speaker: R' Yehoshua
lines.text: It is pure either way — such use always negates its status as a significant garment.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: It depends: prepared for the task, impure; not prepared, pure.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Everyone agrees: thrown in the trash, it is pure. Kept in a box, everyone agrees it is impure. They disagree only over hanging it on a peg or leaving it behind a door.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The wording 'wick of a garment' shows Rabbi Akiva later retracted toward Rabbi Yehoshua's view — it remains a garment only when clearly still valued.

slides.title: 🥚 New Mishna: No Indirect Oil-Drip on Shabbat
slides.subtitle: The Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda disagree on three parallel cases
slides.hebrewSource: לֹא יְמַלֵּא אָדָם קְעָרָה שֶׁל שֶׁמֶן וְיִתְּנֶנָּה בְּצַד הַנֵּר וְיִתֵּן רֹאשׁ הַפְּתִילָה בְּתוֹכָהּ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁתְּהֵא שׁוֹאֶבֶת
slides.label: The mishna:
slides.text: One may not pierce an eggshell (or an earthenware tube), fill it with oil, and set it over the lamp so it drips extra oil in — the Rabbis forbid this even with disgusting earthenware, fearing one might siphon oil directly from it. Rabbi Yehuda permits it. If the vessel-maker attached the tube to the lamp from the start, however, all agree it is permitted, since it is one continuous vessel. Likewise, the Rabbis forbid placing a bowl of oil beside the lamp with the wick's end dipped in to draw more oil; Rabbi Yehuda again permits it.

slides.title: 🏛️ Rabbi Yehuda's Proof — and Its Rejection
slides.subtitle: A story from the house of Nitza in Lod

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda: 'We once spent Shabbat in the upper story of the house of Nitza in Lod, and pierced an eggshell of oil over the lamp — Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders present said nothing.'
2️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda takes their silence as agreement that this is permitted
3️⃣ The Rabbis reject the proof: 'That house's Elders were unusually vigilant' — not representative of ordinary people who might siphon the oil

4️⃣ Lesson drawn (Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar, re: a dragged bench): silence in one exceptional case can wrongly be generalized into leniency — so one must object even when the letter of the law might allow it

nodes.content: ❓ Why did he extinguish the Shabbat lamp?

columns.label: Exempt
columns.content: Fear of gentiles or thieves, an 'evil spirit' (depression), or so a sick person can sleep — not a constructive act

columns.label: Liable
columns.content: To spare the lamp, the oil, or the wick — a constructive, purposeful act

nodes.content: ⚖️ Rabbi Yosei's dissent: exempt in ALL these cases except sparing the wick — since extinguishing it does create something, charcoal

summary.principle: Rabbi Yehuda's ban on kindling with 'broken vessels' (including date pits and nutshells) as nolad, and the parallel bar on indirect oil-feeding devices for the Shabbat lamp, both reflect the Sages' concern for accidental violation, while the new mishna on extinguishing shows that Shabbat liability depends on constructive intent, not the act alone.

flowSteps.content: 🪵 R' Yehuda forbids kindling broken vessels, exposed date pits, and nutshells as 'newly created'; R' Shimon permits all three
🧦 A small cloth's impurity status hinges on whether it was thrown out, boxed, or merely hung up

columns.content: 🥚 Indirect oil-drip devices for the lamp: Rabbis forbid (fear of siphoning), R' Yehuda permits
🪑 Dragging furniture: R' Shimon permits when no furrow is intended

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Extinguishing the Shabbat lamp is exempt when done from fear or for the sick, but liable when done constructively to spare the lamp, oil, or wick

quiz.q: Why did Rav need to teach all three cases — broken vessels, date pits, and nutshells — as separately forbidden by Rabbi Yehuda?
o: Because they involve different Festivals
Because none could be derived from the others: vessels change from whole to broken, pits go from hidden to exposed, and shells were always exposed yet still forbidden
Because only one applies to Shabbat
Because Rabbi Shimon disputes only one of them
quiz.e: Each case demonstrates a different feature that might otherwise have been thought to be the deciding factor, so all three needed to be stated explicitly.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, in what case do Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree about a small cloth's ritual purity?
o: They never agree
Everyone agrees it is pure if thrown into the garbage, and impure if kept in a box; they disagree only about hanging it on a peg or behind a door
They agree only when it was specially prepared
They agree only about wool cloths
quiz.e: The Gemara states that all opinions agree a discarded cloth in the trash is pure and a boxed cloth is impure; the dispute is limited to intermediate cases like hanging it on a peg or behind a door.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, why do the Rabbis forbid piercing an eggshell, filling it with oil, and placing it over the lamp to drip in extra oil?
o: Because eggs may not be used on Shabbat
Because of concern one might come to take oil directly from the dripping vessel, which would hasten extinguishing the lamp
Because it is considered cooking
Because only earthenware is permitted
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' concern is that a person might siphon oil from the vessel, an act akin to accelerating the lamp's extinguishing on Shabbat.

quiz.q: Why did the Rabbis reject Rabbi Yehuda's proof from the silence of Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders in the house of Nitza?
o: Because the story never happened
Because that group of Elders was known to be especially vigilant, unlike ordinary people who might be tempted to siphon the oil
Because Rabbi Tarfon disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda later
Because the house of Nitza was not a valid Shabbat location
quiz.e: The Rabbis explain that the Elders present were unusually careful, so their silence cannot be generalized into a permissive ruling for the general public.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna on extinguishing a lamp, when is one liable rather than exempt?
o: Only when done out of fear
When done to spare the lamp, the oil, or the wick, since these are considered constructive acts
Only when a sick person is disturbed
Never — extinguishing a lamp is always exempt
quiz.e: The mishna states one is exempt for extinguishing out of fear or for the sake of a sick person's sleep, but liable when the intent is to conserve the lamp, oil, or wick — a purposeful, constructive act.
